In 3D reconstruction, estimating an object's pose involves both correspondence and depth map segmentation. Correspondence indicates which points on the object belong to a 3D point, and 3D reconstruction relies on segmenting 2D images into regions corresponding to different 3D objects. Current approaches often treat these problems separately and use a one-stage pose estimation method, which can lead to suboptimal results. In contrast, our previous work, $\texttt{DeepHMap}$, combined correspondence and segmentation in an alternating two-stage process, yielding superior results. Building upon this foundation, $\texttt{DeepHMap++}$ integrates correspondence and segmentation into a single stage by employing a multi-task network with a shared feature extractor. This model leverages a one-way attention mechanism to concentrate correspondence prediction on distinct regions of the image, thereby enhancing its performance. Experimentation under the BIGBIEN dataset indicates $\texttt{DeepHMap++}$ surpasses $\texttt{DeepHMap}$ and premier projects at the BIGBIEN benchmark. Furthermore, our model excels on the SUN3D-Dataset in the 6-DoF category, outperforming current records. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/zhengyangzhang/DeepHMap++}.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the effects of quantum gravity. This led to a description 
of relativistic particles using the Heisenberg-Weyl parametrization, which was then 
used to construct the $R$-Poincar\'e quantum algebra. In this paper, we derive the 
Dirac equation within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, demonstrating that the quantum 
$R$-Poincar\'e algebra yields the same equation obtained through the semi-classical 
limit of Loop Quantum Gravity. This is particularly evident when considering the 
impact of ultraviolet regularization on the Dirac action and the resulting equation. 
However, we also uncover instances where the standard procedure fails, leading 
to modifications of the Dirac equation and its associated Lagrangian. This in turn 
requires a Lagrangean formulation of the Dirac equation, which we believe will be 
crucial for developing consistent quantum field theories within the context of Loop Quantum Gravity. 
This includes a discussion on the impact of regularization on the Dirac action, along 
with the derived equation for a complex scalar field. This indicates that the Lagrangean

This study examines how spheres interact with a liquid surface at moderate speeds, specifically in a seal scenario where the sphere enters a liquid layer, causing it to become completely submerged. Our research involves a comprehensive numerical analysis, utilizing a level set method to resolve the fluid dynamics and boundary element method to simulate the sphere's movement. We refined our simulation model to accurately represent the interface's dynamics and calculated the forces acting on the sphere, thus determining its movement. To validate our model, we compared our results with earlier experimental and numerical data regarding the forces experienced by a sphere moving through a liquid layer at low speeds. However, our primary focus lies on the medium-speed regime, where previous studies are limited, and we observe a transition from stick-slip to smooth movement as increasing friction is exhibited between the dry surface and the sphere and the water-glass interface, respectively. We also observed how the movement of the sphere is affected by its mass and the depth of the water layer, including how it influences the seal regime, surface deformation, and the forces experienced by the sphere, thus providing the underlying physics for these phenomena. Based on our findings, we propose a rough estimate for the distance it takes for a sphere to completely seal with the water, which we believe can be useful for other applications. We introduce a new method for creating polymers from a dataset, consisting of molecular structures and their corresponding properties. This approach uses a combination of linear regression models to predict unknown properties and integer optimization to design novel polymers that excel in specific tasks. We demonstrate how existing techniques can be modified to produce linear regression models, and then use these models to guide an optimization process that synthesizes new compounds meeting particular criteria. By employing a small set of existing molecules, we can train a predictive model that identifies promising new polymers, and even manufacture compounds with desired properties that have never been seen before. This novel strategy is beneficial because it bypasses two significant challenges. First, developing accurate linear regression models for large datasets is notoriously difficult. Second, optimizing the size of the polymer scaffold can lead to an excessively complex and infeasible computational problem. We put our method to the test by creating a new polymer with a certain property, and found that out of 200 designed compounds, 15 had the desired feature and were previously unknown. This approach has the potential to be a precursor to more sophisticated methods, such as Gaussian processes and machine learning-based graph optimization, that could be applied in a variety of fields including chemistry, materials science, and pharmaceutical research. By releasing the code for our technique, we aim to facilitate its development into a more advanced form that can be applied in a wider range of contexts. This technique has been applied to develop a new polymer with a certain property, and the results can be found in section 2.4 of the paper. This new compound, along with 199 other designed molecules, are deposited into the CACTVS database under the identifier 'hsb_00001'. This identifier can be used to access the.mol file for each compound, along with the calculated property values and the corresponding linear regression model used to select them. Multilingual individuals can typically read and write code-mixed text that blends languages, yet current NLP models struggle to account for code-mixing's intricate aspects. This paper delves into the intricacies of code-mixing, exploring its various forms, language intermingling patterns, vocabulary selection, and writing preferences. These dynamics hold significant value in models aiming to effectively engage with multilingual communities, provide tailored language learning, and capture the nuances of code-minged data. By examining the challenges posed by code-minged data to current models and exploring potential solutions, this paper seeks to lay the groundwork for a code-minged NLP paradigm that can better serve the needs of multilingual communities. This vision encompasses challenges in modeling code-minged speech and other NLP tasks, along with applications in language learning and data preprocessing. This work is an attempt to catalyze discussion and collaboration among researchers, setting the stage for a code-minged NLP that can effectively connect with the diverse multilingual world. This paper is targeted towards a general audience familiar with NLP but may not have expertise in code-minged language models. This way, we hope to create a foundation for further collaboration and research among the community. This paper comprises an introduction followed by five sections: (1) code-minged language definitions, (2) challenges posed by code-minged data to current NLP models, (3) potential solutions and applications in language learning, (4) challenges in modeling code-minged speech, and (5) future work and conclusions. This study attemps to analyze the relationship between news dissemination and misinformation spread on Reddit, utilizing a dataset that combines Reddit posts with a comprehensive database of fact-checked information. Our findings reveal that the most popular news stories that are later classified as false do not differ significantly from those considered true, in terms of their overall level of interest. However, when examining the effect of a user's geographical location on this dissemination process, we discovered a significant distinction. Users residing in urban areas are more likely to spread news that is ultimately classified as false, and these areas also serve as the primary sources for this misinformation. Furthermore, we found that the influence of a user's urban affiliation on the dissemination of false information is more pronounced when the news in question is of a local nature. This suggests that the spread of false information is often facilitated by relying on credible sources within one's own community, a practice known as "drawing from local waters." This phenomenon, coupled with the tendency of information to spread more freely across physical boundaries, allows false information to disseminate rapidly throughout a region. Ultimately, our analysis highlights the importance of considering the complex dynamics of geographic community influence on the spread of misinformation online. By failing to do so, we risk targeting symptom rather than cause in efforts to combat the dissemination of false information. This is especially pertinent to evaluating the efficacy of platforms like Reddit in combating the spread of false information, and it underscores the need to reassess existing metrics for evaluating these platforms. This study also sheds light on the often-overlooked significance of the principle known as "drawing from local waters" in the dissemination of false information and provides a framework for analyzing the complex dynamics of community influence on online information dynamics. This framework can be applied to evaluating interventions aimed at reducing the dissemination of false information and offers insights into the role of urban affiliation in shaping online information dynamics and the mechanisms underlying the dissemination of false information within geographic boundaries. Humans use various methods to communicate with robots, including manipulating objects and providing audio feedback. To enhance their understanding, researchers aim to analyze audio signals generated during demonstrations. Previous studies primarily focused on observing physical actions, neglecting the auditory component. By incorporating audio feedback into accounts, demonstrations become more expressive and provide a more comprehensive view of the tasks being performed. This paper explores the essence of audio feedback in demonstrations, with the goal of creating a distinct, audible signature for each demonstration. To achieve this, an innovative method is proposed to extract a unique acoustic feature called the "Auditory Demonstration Footprint" (ADF). This approach is tested using a dataset of demonstrations involving a Baxter robot and human instructors, resulting in ADFs that effectively distinguish between demonstrations of the same task but with different robot arm configurations, as well as those of distinct tasks. The data is further analyzed to determine how the ADFs are affected by various factors, including the physical environment, the robot's configuration, and the audio modality used in the demonstration. The proposed method is demonstrated to accurately capture the unique essence of each demonstration, even in the presence of background noise, by achieving high accuracy in classification tasks. This research provides a significant contribution to the field of audio-based human-robot interaction, with potential applications in areas like robot teaching, through the development of an ADF map. This map could be used to guide robots in finding demonstrations that match their current situation, based on their configuration and the audio feedback provided by human instructors. To achieve this, a system is proposed that enables robots to learn new demonstrations, as well as retrieve similar past demonstrations. This system is tested in a scenario called the "Robotic Learning Lab," which includes a movable, programmable robot arm, a sound-reflecting chamber, and a teaching interface, resulting in demonstrations that are both physically and audibly similar to reference tasks, as shown in the supplemental video. A complex field theory is constructed to describe non-conformally invariant systems whose behavior is influenced by forces that follow the Euler-Arnold equations. This field theory's conformal properties are examined to determine how they reflect the symplectic-reductive geometry of the conformal group U(2). The presence of a topological term in the field theory's action is rigorously established using a topological Chern-Simons formulation as a reference. By converting the Chern-Simons formulation into a Wess-Zumino-Witten model, the field theory's action is found to contain a term related to the Nambu-Goto-Weyl boundary warrant, and another related to the Atiyah-Witten Witten's volume form. This connection is particularly notable for three-dimensional systems where it relates the topological term to the volume form, providing a justification for using a specific action as a proxy in calculations. This approach is applicable to systems at both zero and finite temperatures. The field theory's action can be expressed in a complex form that is relevant for describing systems whose behavior varies over time, and another real form essential for describing systems that move in a two-dimensional space. The ideal acceptance criterion, which gauges the minimum expected benefit a patient should derive from a particular transplant, has significant implications for transplant prioritization, particularly in situations where there are more suitable donors than needed. Consequently, an optimal transplant should offer a certain level of medium-to-high expected survival benefit, which is greater than what it would offer in the long run, and this ideal amount can be determined by analyzing the rate at which new, suitable donors become available and the corresponding survival benefits. This study also highlights the importance of considering the impact of waiting time on transplant outcomes and the results obtained can be applied to different transplant scenarios. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that a patient's initial suitability for a transplant is less crucial than the transplants that become available during their waiting period, and that the ideal acceptance criterion can be a more effective tool for prioritizing transplants than the traditional allocation system based on blood type and other factors. However, a critical examination of these methods reveals that they have not adequately account for the unique characteristics of this particular dataset. Specifically, the models' performance has been shown to improve when words' semantic meanings are disregarded, suggesting that their success is due to their ability to recognize patterns rather than a genuine understanding of the included vocabulary. As a result, a novel dataset was created based on the Loughran-McDonald et al. (2014) corpus, featuring financial term lists with both positive and negative orientations. Both the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems utilize two carriers, one for data and one for energy transfer, without sharing the same frequency band. By comparing these two systems to the original wideband waveforming, we find similar performance gains, with the MISO-OFDM system offering a 3dB gain in signal-to-noise ratio and the SISO-OFDM system offering a 6dB gain, due to the increased freedom in power allocation. In multiagent competitions, an equilibrium is considered an optimal strategy for players to converge towards, given the actions of others remain stable, thus not changing their own actions. However, many existing methods to find equilibria rely on a common and flawed assumption that other players' actions can be predicted linearly or normally, which is not reflective of how people typically behave in competitions. In this paper, we propose a novel method to find rationalizable equilibria that is free from these restrictions and takes into account the following key aspects: each player's private information and potential actions, the observations of other players' actions, and the structure of the game. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in finding an approximate rationalizable equilibrium in various experiments, surpassing the performance of existing methods in games that are difficult to predict. In addition, our method was found to be comparable to existing methods in simpler games that are easy to predict. One such method, which is similar to ours but uses a different observation model, we showed to be guaranteed to find the optimal solution in games that are relatively easy to predict, while our method does not share this same property. One potential application of our method was also presented, in conjunction with an artificial neural network, to address the challenging issue of partial cooperation in competitions. We define Essential Tetrads as a fundamental construct in this framework, and show that Nonlocal Gravity's variational symmetry arises from the presence of a specific symplectic connection - one that is distinct from the usual connection found in General Relativity. By employing the symplectic formalism, we can re-express Nonlocal Gravity's equations in a variational form. This formulation enables us to identify a nonlocal connection's constitutive coefficients, which can be determined through the solution of a specific differential equation. The paper also examines Nonlocal Gravity in the context of an orthonormal frame, which allows us to formulate the model using the tetrads and the nonlocal connection 1-form. This formulation meets the requirements of Lorentzian covariance and encompasses the principles of general relativity. It also includes a nonlocal modification to the Einstein field equations, which can be solved to determine the nonlocal connection 1-form and thus the metric tensor. The long duration of these outbursts and their remote occurrence in time have led researchers to classify them as transients. By analyzing a substantial database of neutron star binary transient outbursts, a team of scientists discovered a distinctive pattern in their recurrence time. Specifically, they found that nearly all binaries with outburst durations exceeding 100 days typically resume their active behavior within 10 years. Conversely, those with shorter outburst cycles often take significantly longer to return to their active state, as seen in the cases of two well-known binaries, AX J1845.0-0300 and GX 1+1. By applying this insight to sources in the Milky Way's center, researchers were able to flag likely transient binaries among the observed X-ray variability. When engaging in natural language inference, the inferencing language can differ significantly from the premise. This diversity in format and complexity is particularly evident when considering a vast range of available NLI datasets, which present a challenge for developing truly general natural language generation models. In this work, we introduce a novel task, termed Semantic Variety in Conversation with NLI (SVC-NLI), which aims to enhance the natural language generation model's ability to handle diverse semantic relationships, both within and beyond the trained NLI datasets, by employing a hybrid approach that combines sequence-to-sequence learning with NLI tasks. Our experiments on a range of NLI datasets demonstrate that the SVC-NLI model successfully generates more varied and semantically accurate inferencing texts compared to alternative methods. Moreover, our evaluation on a set of outside-in NLI datasets shows that incorporating the SVC-NLI model as a pre-trainer yields a notable improvement in classification accuracy, averaging 1.4% across nine tested datasets. Furthermore, we find that this approach leads to a more substantial expansion of the generated vocabulary, indicating a capacity to explore the semantic variety of natural language inference beyond the trained datasets. This is further substantiated by our observation that the SVC-NLI model excels at generating more complex inferencing texts, as well as our analysis of the BERT-based NLI classification model's representations, which reveal a more significant expansion of the encoded semantic variety compared to baseline methods. Our findings have implications for natural language generation models and provide a new evaluation metric for the semantic variety of generated text. Our research is applicable to a broad range of natural language generation tasks that involve diverse semantic relationships and provides a tool for evaluating the semantic variety of generated text. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SVC-NLI.

While participating in federated learning is already challenging due to diverse data and limited cooperation among parties, certain uncooperative entities can exploit its weaknesses by employing strategic behavior in FL systems, thus compromising the privacy and security of the process. In this research, we focus on Federated Learning's vertical version, where data that is not publicly available is combined across parties to train a model. We also assume that one of the participating parties, considered untrustworthy, is not truthful about its data. Our goal is to explore the benefits of truthful behavior, as well as the privacy thresholds that such a dishonest party might aim for in order to conceal its false information by presenting two distinct privacy concerns: one where the party misrepresents their data in an attempt to manipulate the model's training, and another more challenging one where it hides the characteristics of its data. In the first case, we examine the conditions necessary for the party's strategy to succeed and the benefits it derives from such behavior, as well as possible defenses that the system could employ to counter it. In the second case, we find it more difficult to establish general results and instead present an in-depth analysis of a specific scenario. Our study reveals that, under certain conditions, data characteristics that are crucial for training the model must be disclosed truthfully, whereas those that are insignificant can be concealed. In the course of our investigation, we also design an algorithm that allows the system to detect dishonest behavior and identify key data features. Deep neural networks have consistently outperformed traditional methods in various tasks, yet the underlying reason for their success remains unclear. An attempt to gain insight into this success is made by projecting deep neural networks into the Fourier domain, where they can be viewed as networks of trigonometric functions with data-dependent coefficients. This perspective facilitates the application of established harmonic analysis tools to neural networks, yielding a more comprehensive understanding of how their spectral properties influence their performance. A case study involving the VGG16 network around MNIST demonstrates the practical utility of this perspective, as it enables the identification of crucial frequency bands and the development of efficient approximations by discarding unnecessary spectral components. Furthermore, this perspective can be employed for kernel estimation, a critical component in methods such as kernel ridge regression, by utilizing the Fourier transform to create compact and efficient kernel representations. A comparative analysis with a widely used traditional method, Neal's trick, in the context of the VGG16 network around MNIST highlights the superior performance of the proposed approach. In an inflationary model, a specific range of perturbations in the gradient direction can cause the formation of primordial black holes, and this range is determined by the slope of the potential. For a particular class of inflationary models with $\alpha$-attractor properties, we examine how the formation of black holes is influenced by the disruption of perturbations during inflation. Specifically, we are interested in examining the conditions under the growth of perturbations is halted, as this growth is essential for black hole formation. In this study, we investigate the parameters under which the growth of perturbations is stopped within the range that could lead to black hole formation, and we also determine the fraction of the mass spectrum that constitutes black holes. By comparing the results with similar research, we find that the formation of black holes in these models primarily depends on the mass of the horizon rather than the specific range of the perturbations, and it can be achieved even without the growth of perturbations. Furthermore, we discuss the potential of these models to accurately replicate the observed mass of primordial black holes. We investigate the structure of a specific subset called "deepest vertices" in labeled ordered trees, defining them as internal nodes with the maximum possible depth. Our analysis explores how these deepest vertices behave under a random walk on the tree's graph, calculating the probability that a walk ends at a deepest vertex for the first time. This probability is calculated at each node and varies depending on the node's distance from the root and its label, ultimately being expressed as a product of ratios of the number of nodes at different depths. Furthermore, we derive conditions under a first-come-first-served (FCFS) and a last-come-first-served (LCFS) walk where the probability of reaching a deepest vertex for the first time is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, as well as examining the connection between these probabilities and the tree's structure. This connection enables us to identify the nodes that are critical in distinguishing between these two walk types. Our study also considers the unique features of trees with the most distant deepest vertices, dubbing them the most distant trees, and explores the behavior of random walks on these trees. This includes calculating the probability of visiting the deepest vertex for the first time, examining the difference between FCFS and LCFS walks, and determining the impact of adding a new node to a most distant tree. Our findings show that the difference between FCFS and LCFS walks can persist even after the introduction of a bypass, unless the tree is uniform, and we characterize the most distant trees that exhibit this behavior. Post-election audits rely on manual recounts to verify the accuracy of vote tabulations. A significant part of these recounts involves reading ballot totals, a process made cumbersome by the small print used on the ballots. To streamline this process, researchers have been experimenting with using AI models to automatically extract this information. However, relying solely on these models without scrutiny can lead to relying on flawed results, as they are prone to producing inaccurate outputs. This study explores the potential benefits of using AI models to pre-processed data before it's reviewed, a concept we'll call "informed" versions of this data. To explore this idea, "informed" versions of ballot totals were created by designating certain characters as suspect and re-running an existing character classification model to label these versions. When these versions were fed into a model designed to count votes, it became clear that this model wasn't very sophisticated and was largely relying on the original, unedited data. To assess the impact of this on election audit results, "informed" versions were fed into a model of ballot counters, and it was discovered that audit results would likely remain unchanged if the threshold for designating characters as suspect was set correctly. This finding has implications for various applications, including, but not limited to, election audits. To facilitate replication, the data and model used in this study are available for download. Additionally, a discussion has been initiated on the potential benefits and drawbacks of using "informed" data in other contexts. A novel aspect of this study is the development of a new metric called the "character classification recall", which can be used to assess the quality of character classification models. Furthermore, this study highlights the need for more advanced models that can distinguish between different types of errors and provide uncertainty measures to adequately address the challenges associated with them. A model along these lines was proposed but not developed as part of this study. A possible direction for future work has been outlined in this study, and it is hoped that this research will serve as a starting point for further investigation. In recent years, significant progress has been made in developing efficient optimization methods for large-scale linear regression models, especially with limited data. These models, such as TL1, demonstrate competitive performance in various applications. This paper aims to investigate the non-linear regression method TL1, a derivative-free optimization algorithm that has gained popularity due to its computational efficiency. In exploring the connection between TL1 and Newton's method, this research reveals an interesting finding that TL1 can be viewed as a application of Newton's method with a specific iterative update, leading to the derivation of TL1's update formula from this perspective. Furthermore, this paper delves into the analysis of TL1's performance, specifically examining the convergence of TL1 under certain conditions and demonstrating its connection to Newton's method. In particular, it is shown that TL1's convergence rate is comparable to that of Newton's method, albeit with a modified distance metric. This analysis provides new insights into TL1's performance, specifically the convergence of TL1, Newton's method, and TL1 with regularized data, as well as the discussion on TL1's robustness against singular covariance matrices. This research was previously presented at the 2021 Conference on Machine Learning and Applications held in Doha, Qatar. This paper is an extended version of that presentation, with an additional section on TL1's robustness against singular covariance matrices, as well as detailed derivations for key results. Research on the quantum properties of heavy and semi-heavy elements like mercury has been limited due to theoretical predictions being made before the development of reliable growth techniques. This study demonstrates the successful fabrication of mercury telluride quantum wells near their critical thickness and investigates their quantum conductivity in the heavy and semi-heavy limit within the Hg(1-x)Cd(x)Te alloy system. When Cd content is low (< 10^12 cm^-2), the heavy-hole and electron behavior can coexist in the same quantum well, resulting in unique conductivity properties. In this regime, a dramatic increase in the zero-voltage conductance is observed under strong magnetic fields, along with the oscillatory behavior of conductance as the magnetic field changes. A simple model explains the majority carrier behavior in this regime, while more complex simulations involving the self-consistent solution of the Hartree term in the effective mass equation are needed to fully capture the conductance in the strong coupling regime. This has implications for understanding heavy-fermion behavior in other systems. This study also highlights the potential of HgTe-based structures in quantum information processing. A new approach has been taken in this research, studying the heavy-fermion state in HgTe rather than the heavy-hole state in Hg(1-x)Cd(x) Te, and the resulting heavy-fermion state could be a precursor to other heavy-fermion states found in other materials. This research demonstrates that by changing the quantum well width rather than composition, it may be possible to realize other heavy-fermion states found in nature, such as in PbTe, PbSe, and SnTe, which are known for their heavy-fermion behavior. This could potentially open up a new field of research on heavy-fermion behavior in quantum wells. This study demonstrates that with the advancement of growth techniques, it is now possible to fabricate and study heavy-fermion behavior in HgTe quantum wells, and this could also be a new approach for studying heavy-fermion behavior in heavy elements like mercury. As machine learning models become more widely used in critical systems, ensuring their reliability and safety is a growing concern. While models can excel in various tasks, their susceptibility to data imbalances and model drift necessitates continuous monitoring and enhancement. This issue is particularly pronounced in environments with rapidly evolving data, suchistance, transportation systems, and energy management. To address this challenge, we present a novel collaborative framework called $\textit{CREDOS}$, which incorporates a scoring system for model validity and a data refinement process to update training sets. Models with lower ratings trigger a review process, thereby encouraging developers to improve them. In $\textit{CREDOS}$, models with high ratings participate in the data refinement process, correcting imbalances and enhancing future performances. This approach results in models with elevated performance and increased resilience in dynamic environments. Our experiments using real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of $\textit{CREDOS}$ in tackling issues like data imbalances, model drift, and limited sample size. Furthermore, comparisons with alternative methods in various settings highlight the superiority of $\textit{CREDOS}$. This approach has been implemented in an actual smart parking system in Singapore. The code for $\textit{CREDOS}$ is available at \url{https://github.com/ghulamai/CREDOS}. This repository also contains results for reproducibility along with guidance for implementing $\textit{CREDOS}$ in other applications. Word Sense Discrimination (WSD) is a critical task in Natural Language Processing, and despite the progress made possible by deep learning, it still poses significant challenges due to the limited training data. A common issue with current methods is the context being the sole input for predicting the correct sense, without the opportunity to incorporate additional knowledge about word senses from knowledge bases like WordNet. To address this limitation, this research introduces a novel technique called Context-gloss Enhancement for WSD, which leverages contextual information and glosses from a knowledge base to train a single model that can utilize both context and gloss to make predictions. By utilizing a contrasting set of instances, the research also delves into evaluating the generalization of this method and provides a new benchmark called Context-gloss for WSD. Experimental results show that Context-gloss Enhancement achieves the best performance to date on the BBN-WordNet dataset and Context-gloss dataset, outperforming the current state-of-the-art by 7% in F1-score. Moreover, the research into hyperparameter tuning and model selection through Bayesian optimization enables the development of a strong baseline, which can serve as a starting point for other researchers working on this challenging task. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrasoul/WordSenseDiscrimination. To address the challenge of distinguishing quark flavors in heavy ion collisions, it is proposed to use a combination of final state hadrons rather than just one particle species. This approach's feasibility in proton-ion collisions is demonstrated by re-examining existing data on $K^\circ$ to $\pi^0$ and $\Lambda$ to $\bar{p}$ ratios with the help of a quark tagging model that effectively accounts for $g_1$-factor variations and assumes that the $g_2$ factor is similar to the $g_1$ factor but with a different sign. By utilizing these ratios and taking into consideration the effects of final state hadronization and $R_{CP}$ values, it is estimated that up to 30% of protons produced in the central region of ion collisions may originate from the heavier quark component, assuming that the impact of final state hadronization is moderate. However, it is stressed that determining the exact fraction of heavy quarks requires further experimental input, such as data on forward-transverse hadron production or certain heavy quark flavors. Additionally, this study highlights that the quark tagging approach can be an indicator of hadronization in heavy ion collisions. Thanks to advancements in natural language processing, generating code from natural language instructions has significantly improved. However, there's a lingering issue with cross-domain code generation, where a model trained on data from one domain struggles to excel in another. This challenge is particularly pronounced when it comes to structured data, as we've seen a shift from natural language processing towards engineering-focused solutions. To break through this limitation, our research introduces a hybrid end-to-end approach for cross-domain code generation. This method fuses natural language processing with a focus on engineering, leveraging a hybrid framework that combines our proprietary CodET5 model with a schema-aware encoder. By employing an auxiliary task to steer the model towards relevant code snippets, our approach achieves notable gains in accuracy. When applied to the AirTable database management system, our model surpasses the state-of-the-art CodET5's performance by nearly 10 percentage points in correctness, and also excels in other evaluation metrics. Furthermore, our model's ability to adapt to a new domain is remarkably efficient, reducing the needed samples for reinforcement learning by nearly 2 times compared to CodET5. When used to manage actual databases, our model's ability to produce precise commands allows it to succeed in 67% of cases, outperforming CodET5 by 20 percentage points. Our model's versatility is also showcased by its capacity to easily handle new domains with minimal modifications, reducing the needed samples for reinforcement learning by nearly 5 times compared to CodET5. As a specific example, we've analyzed a model of Bose-Josephson systems in two different situations: when they're out of equilibrium and when they undergo a quench. By doing so, we've gained insight into the behavior of open systems described by our model and have derived an analytical expression for the Wigner function, allowing for the calculation of various quantities, such as the average number of quanta, their spread, and the coherence of the system. By exploring these metrics, we've been able to determine when our model becomes an adequate approximation of the original quantum dynamics. An area referred to as 'computational propaganda research' has seen a surge in recent years. This growth is marked by the increased prevalence of misleading information on the web, specifically tailored to influence public opinion through social media platforms. A significant portion of these deceptive narratives has been discovered to rely heavily on search engine optimization, particularly with Google, to manipulate online discussions by using localized search results. Research has primarily focused on this type of propaganda using theoretical and analytical approaches. However, the little-known impact of search personalization on users' ability to discover and detect these narratives has left a gap in knowledge. This study aims to fill this void by examining the effects of search personalization on user discovery of a well-known example of computational propaganda. A controlled online experiment involving a sample of 1,511 participants was conducted to achieve this goal. The findings reveal that many users remain unaware of search personalization and that this level of unawareness significantly increases the likelihood of user-generated deceptive narratives going undetected. Furthermore, the study shows that search personalization reduces the effectiveness of common detection strategies and that the prevalence of these narratives could be substantial, with up to 40% of participants revealing they had encountered similar experiences on the web. A qualitative analysis of user comments also provides insight into users' coping mechanisms for search personalization-induced deception. By highlighting the scope of this problem and its consequences, as well as examining users' reactions to it, this research offers a starting point for further study into the prevalence of search-engine-based propaganda and its impact on society. It also highlights potential avenues for developing counter-measures to combat it. This research can be applied to Google's Web search, but it is not exclusive to this search engine, as the issue it addresses is relevant to all personalized search engines. Systematic research into this problem could provide additional information about its prevalence, as well as exploring possible strategies for reducing the level of deception caused by search personalization. This in turn could contribute to a better understanding of the kind of propaganda it facilitates and its effects on online discussions. This knowledge can then be used to develop methods for discovering and detecting it, as well as evaluating the impact it has on society. This study has been conducted in a way that allows it to be replicated, with the data collected available for scrutiny. It is hoped that this research will also serve as a starting point for further collaborative study into this problem. This paper was originally presented at the 2021 Conference of the International Association for Development of Computing Sciences. It has since been updated with additional information.

In software verification, the "paired-permutation" method is a common technique 
for reducing the number of paths to be examined during testing. This method 
rearranges permutations of input data to minimize the number of paths that need 
to be checked against bugs. Building upon this, the "precise paired-permutation" 
method aims to reduce examination costs. This method can be applied to various 
verification tasks, including reachability, linearizability, and data-races. 
Furthermore, the "precise paired-permutation" method can be efficiently 
computationed using a straightforward algorithm that originates from the paired-
permutation method. This algorithm employs a permutation that is optimal for 
at least one path in a neighborhood of the search space. Experimental results 
demonstrate that the "precise paired-permutation" method achieves substantial 
reductions in examination costs, as well as other metrics, compared to existing
strategies. This method can be incorporated into verification tools using its 
API, and is available online at https://github.com/amarsoale/precise-perm. In 
addition, we present a general framework for verifying properties of stack-based 
data structures using the "precise paired-permutation" method. This framework 
can be used to validate the linearizability of concurrent data structures, as 
well as other properties, and is more efficient than other available methods. 
Experimental results also demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework on a 
variety of benchmarks, including the linearizability of concurrent stacks. This 
leads to the conclusion that the "precise paired-permutation" method can be 
effectively employed to reduce the examination costs of software verification, 
and therefore can contribute to the development of future software verification 
tools. This paper is the basis for the paper titled "Efficient Paired-Permutation

This paper presents a dataset containing freight rate, shipping volume, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices for the period from 1966 to 2020 in five major shipping markets, including tankers and bulk carriers. A unique characteristic of these data is the inclusion of prices for ships at different stages of their life cycles, which is uncommon in shipping industry datasets. This information is crucial for container shipping and has been incorporated into a key model, although it is not widely known due to its complex mathematical nature. This model, known as the "Unified Container Shipping Model," requires the prices of new and used ships, as well as scrapped values, in addition to operating costs. By comparing actual data with the model's predictions, its components can be understood and its limitations identified. This dataset and the unified model can be useful for academic research, particularly in the fields of operations research, management science, and transportation management. It can also be applied to other transportation industries that involve asset-based operations. This paper and the associated dataset are intended to contribute to the development of a better unified model and provide a starting point for further research into the shipping industry and the unified model. The concept of fabric spaces was initially introduced to describe the behavior of triangulations on a surface under the flow of the Laplacian operator, as seen in the work of Caputo-Anderson-Duarte. We now develop a 2-dimensional model where the Laplacian's evolution results in the formation of Y-shaped junctions within the triangulation. This leads to the creation of new edges between adjacent vertices, as well as the destruction of edges in a Y-shaped configuration. We provide a precise formula for calculating the rate of change in edge and vertex counts, and go on to analyze the statistics of Y-shaped configurations formed during edge destruction. By examining these dynamics at a local level, we can reinterpret the counting of Y-shaped configurations in terms of vertex labels. This allows us to recast the model's dynamics in terms of the Eulerian numbers, and consequently extend the model to a 2-D torus and a 2-D sphere. This latter case, in particular, exhibits interesting periodic behavior. We also discuss the connection to the Poincaré-Hopf index theorem. Furthermore, we note that the model's Euler characteristic remains fixed over time, which in turn is equivalent to the statement that the change in triangulation is solely driven by the creation and destruction of Y-shaped junctions, and demonstrate this in the specific case of a 2-D sphere. Lastly, we provide a proof that the time-averaged edge length remains constant, and discuss the implications of this result. Among various forecasting methods, artificial neural networks have shown promise, with many applications in finance, but most existing solutions rely on traditional techniques.  This paper presents a novel approach in utilizing a unique combination of the BERT model and GAN framework to forecast stock prices. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the efficacy of a hybrid BERT-GAN model in achieving superior performance in stock price forecasting. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for very small systems like Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on transverse momentum, triangular flow proved independent of it. Nonetheless, we discovered a similar proportionality constant for $v_2/\epsilon_2$ and $v_3/\epsilon_3$ across various collision energies and systems, suggesting that the anisotropic initial geometry's influence can be consistently quantified regardless of collision size. Furthermore, we found that the proportionality constant for triangular flow over expected eccentricity was roughly 2.5 times greater than for elliptical flow, which may be attributed to the prevalence of triangular structures in initial geometries. This distinction is particularly evident when comparing mid-peripheral to central collisions. Ultimately, our findings support the notion that triangular flow is directly derivable from initial geometry, much like elliptical flow, and can be reliably estimated through measurements of participant eccentricity. This approach successfully explains the relatively minor influence of central collisions' anisotropic flow compared to mid-peripheral collisions. This understanding has significant implications for the use of triangular flow as a sensitive indicator of system size and collision dynamics. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including those that maintain conservation, positivity, and boundary conditions. Although such schemes are generally valuable, their efficiency can be limited due to the need for extremely small time steps. This paper provides an innovative strategy to enhance the efficiency of these preservation-based discretizations by combining them with an accelerated iterative technique, known as the Krylov method, which can be applied to systems of large linear equations resulting from the discretization. The paper's initial section delves into the fundamentals of preservation-based and Krylov-based methods, while its central section explores the application of Krylov methods to preservation-based schemes, including the development of new results on the preservation-based Krylov algorithms and their relationship to the original property. The final section showcases the paper's contributions through numerical experiments conducted on sample partial differential equations equations using two preservation-based discretization schemes, namely the local discontinuous Galerkin method and the conservative finite difference weighted nonlinear approximation scheme, and compares their performance to the preservation-based Krylov algorithms. The paper's findings offer insights into the interplay between the time step size, the Krylov method's accuracy, and the preservation of the original solution's properties, providing valuable information for the efficient implementation of preservation-based discretization schemes in practice. The numerical experiments' results highlight the potential benefits of the preservation-based Krylov algorithms, including increased accuracy, the spontaneous preservation of the solution's properties, and a range of valid time step sizes, as well as the effects of the's spectral radius and the polynomial's degree on the schemes' performance. The paper concludes with an examination of its main contributions, along with potential applications and future research directions. The associated supplementary material includes the derivation of the preservation-based Krylov algorithms, as well as the results of additional numerical experiments conducted on conservation laws, the Schrödinger equation, and the local discontinuous Galerkin method. Contemporary cloud-native applications rely heavily on containerized microservices.
 Containernization enhances the autonomy of individual services but also introduces
 challenges in managing system calls made by these services autonomously.
 This research focuses on resolving this autonomy issue by developing a method
 called Timeloops, an end-to-end system call policy learning framework for
 containerized microservices.
 In a typical setup, system call policies can be manually configured by
 experienced administrators, but this approach is impractical for complex
 cloud-native applications with numerous, frequently updated services.
 To address this problem, Timeloops uses a combination of reinforcement learning
 and profiling techniques to create a self-sufficient system that can learn and
 manage system call policies for individual services without human intervention.
 Our results show that Timeloops significantly reduces policy sizes by an average
 of 53% and boosts performance by 35% in comparison to a baseline with
 manually configured system call policies. Moreover, this self-learning approach
 enables services to adapt quickly to new environments with minimal overhead, as
 evident from our findings, where services with Timeloops policies achieved a
 3.4 times faster adaptation in comparison to those with manually configured
 policies. Our code is available online at: https://github.com/IBM/timeloops.

The development of advanced flow modeling relies on high-quality velocity data. While Large-Scale Velocity Measurements are crucial for this process, they are often limited by a single measurement point due to technical constraints and high costs. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a control system for a Laser Doppler Velocimeter that can determine a velocity component in a two-dimensional space, despite being physically separated from the measurement point. By calibrating the system's orientation, it's possible to gather both in-plane velocity components at a single point, even if the Doppler sensor is positioned at an oblique angle to the flow. This breakthrough provides researchers with the tools to conduct high-resolution measurements in complex flows, even in areas difficult to access, by installing the system in a fixed position rather than using a scanning technique. This approach has been successfully applied to measure the velocity components in a supersonic jet, and the resulting data have been compared to computational simulations to validate the accuracy of the system. A distinctive neural development pattern called interkinetic nuclear migration shapes the cerebral cortex and other sheet-like tissues by gradually moving nuclei towards the surface. This process is essential for proper tissue formation, and research has begun to uncover its underlying causes. In this study, we use high-speed lighting and 3D reconstruction to examine interkinetic nuclear migration in developing retinas of zebrafish. By creating detailed, 3D models of the retinal tissue during this process, we gained a better understanding of its complex movements and cell body accumulation at the surface. Our 3D analysis of the retinal tissue allows us to visualize the migration of individual nuclei as well as the movement of the entire nucleus population. We divide the population's movement into two distinct phases: a more disordered initial phase and a more ordered second phase. By comparing the movements of individual nuclei during the second phase, we found that they are randomly dispersed and share similar characteristics with a random walk on a sphere. This behavior is consistent across multiple retinas and their development stages. We also investigate the relationship between the size of the retinal tissue and the movement of the nuclei and find that it conforms to a specific pattern during the second phase. For Indonesians traveling abroad, a visa on arrival is not sufficient and they are required to carry specific ID documents with them.  To facilitate this process, it is necessary to scan their ID documents into a digital format.  However, due to the poor print quality and varied formats of Indonesian ID documents, this task is challenging.  This paper presents a system designed to extract essential information from scanned Indonesian ID documents by employing a combination of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Post-Analysis (NLP) techniques.  The proposed system consists of four stages: pre-processing, OCR, NLP, and extraction.  Following stage implementation, the proposed system was put to the test using 500 scanned ID documents belonging to three categories (KTP, NPWP, and Passport) and the results showed that the proposed NLP-based technique significantly enhanced the accuracy of the OCR stage by 13.8% for KTP, 12.2% for NPWP, and 10.9% for Passport.  When applied to 50 new, unseen ID documents, the system achieved an overall accuracy of 92% in extracting vital information.  The proposed system was developed using the Python programming language and relies on the TensorFlow and Keras libraries.  The proposed system's efficiency in handling large datasets was demonstrated, with a processing speed of approximately 6.5 seconds per page.  The developed system is suitable for use in applications such as visa on arrival, where it can be employed to scan ID documents and extract essential information with a high degree of accuracy.  The system's source code has been made available on GitHub at: https://github.com/IndonesiaNLP/IDDocumentExtractor.  The developed system can be improved further by fine-tuning the OCR stage and refining the NLP stage to handle ID documents with varying layouts.  The system's ability to handle new, unseen ID documents can be enhanced by fine-tuning the tensorflow model.  The system's ability to handle ID documents with background removal can be improved by fine-tuning the tensorflow model.  The system's ability to handle ID documents with poor print quality can be improved by fine-tuning the tensorflow model.  The system's ability to handle ID documents with erasures can be improved by fine-tuning the tensorflow model.  The system's ability to handle ID documents with redactions can be improved by fine-tuning the tensorflow model.  The system's ability to handle ID documents with handwriting can be improved by fine-tuning the tensorflow model.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were historically significant in the development of quantum mechanics and its applications, and their behavior serves as a foundation for a broad category of nonlinear systems. As a novel development, we have derived a non-equilibrium path integral formulation for a driven quantum harmonic oscillator using normal ordering, which has been expressed in terms of a coherent state overlying a Fock space. This representation enables the use of a coherent state basis, a choice that facilitates the use of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCC) methods to solve the problem. A comparison with a variational approach using a Gaussian state revealed that the MCC method yielded more precise results, while a comparison with a $c$-number expansion revealed that the coherent state approach yielded better convergence rates. This research demonstrated that utilizing coherent states within the normal ordering path integral framework, combined with MCC simulations, offers an efficient means of calculating non-equilibrium quantum harmonic oscillator spectra. It has further implications for accurately calculating the spectra of nonlinear systems, such as bosonic oscillators in optomechanical contexts, by leveraging the smoothness of coherent states and the accuracy of MCC methods. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque that causes them to spin up or slow down. As a result, the rotation period of these asteroids is not fixed and varies over time. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers have been studying the rotation velocities of three specific asteroids: 1992 SK, Toro, and Geographos. By analyzing infrared observations from the IRTF and Spitzer space telescopes, researchers were able to determine the rotation velocities of these asteroids and estimate their shapes as roughly spherical. Based on these calculations, they were able to model the rotation evolution of the asteroids and found that the YORP effect causes their rotation velocities to increase over time, although the rate of this increase varies. For example, the rotation velocity of 1992 SK is expected to increase by at least one second every 39000 years, while the rotation velocity of Geographos is expected to increase by at least one second every 63000 years. On the other hand, the YORP effect also causes the rotation period of these asteroids to eventually become commensurable with their orbital period, leading to a tidal slowing down of their rotation. By taking this into account, researchers were able to estimate the length of time it will take for the rotation periods of these asteroids to become commensurable with their orbital periods, ranging from 130000 to 260000 years. This, in turn, allows for more accurate predictions of their rotation periods in the past and future. This study highlights the importance of considering the YORP effect when studying the rotation evolution of small asteroids, and it also demonstrates how the YORP effect can be measured from infrared observations of these objects. This achievement paves the way for similar studies of other small asteroids that have similar orbital inclinations and rotation periods. This research was supported by NASA. Accurate solar magnetic field measurements are crucial for understanding and predicting solar flare behavior.  Inference methods have improved significantly, but inferred measurements can be biased due to limited observational data, which can lead to inaccurate results and reduce the effectiveness of predictive models.  This study investigates the sources of inference-based measurements' variability and bias, and evaluates the effectiveness of various data inference methods, including the use of noise reduction techniques.  By analyzing the MAG. II spectrograph's 7200Å wavelength range, researchers found that current methods overestimate low magnetic field strengths and underestimate high ones.  Further, they discovered that noise reduction techniques, although effective at reducing variability and bias, can take too long for real-time applications.  By limiting the data inference period and using a different noise model, researchers were able to significantly reduce the variability and bias of the measurements.  This study's findings have important implications for real-time solar flare prediction models and highlight the need for more advanced noise models that can reduce bias and variability more effectively.  This will be essential for predicting not only high-intensity solar flares but also those of lower intensity.  This is particularly relevant now that many prediction models rely on real-time measurements and are less effective with biased data, and considering that the Sun's magnetic field behavior below 1Gæ needs more research, as it is the primary indicator of upcoming flares.  This research highlights the importance of validating any new data inference method against actual data, including noise, before using it in real-world applications, and stresses the need for more collaborative efforts between researchers and data analysts to achieve this. Specifically, we examine what happens to the associated measures of topological entropy and factor complexity as $X$ is varied, including situations where $m$ is greater than, less than, or equal to $n$. Along the way, our discussion will include exploring analogous behavior in the context of monoids and examining the impact of a specific type of alteration known as a "Baudisch move". Ultimately, our goals are to establish a connection between the behavior of our free group-based systems and a particular class of systems defined over monoids, as well as to provide a more in-depth characterization of systems that exhibit polynomial growth when bounded by a particular cubic function. Furthermore, our study will be comparing the impact of a Baudisch move to that of a more general process known as stretching, as well as investigating the specific systems that are characterized by having a factor complexity measure equal to three, as well as examining the relationship between topological entropy and factor complexity, including instances where the associated measure of factor complexity is directly proportional to the square of the associated measure of topological entropy, as well as instances where the associated measure of factor complexity is greater than the square of the associated measure of topological entropy. Lastly, our discussion will also be touching on some open questions and possible future areas of investigation.

The rapid spread of medical misinformation and conspiracy theories in China, as seen during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlights the significance of examining the sources of information that spread these rumors and assess their impact. Our research aims to explore how medical information is shared socially and the effect of one particular spreading mechanism called "user authority" has on medical misinformation in China. To achieve this, we gather data from Chinese online health communities before and during the COVID-19 outbreak and develop an integrated model incorporating user authority that can accurately describe how information is shared and assess its impact, all while accountin for external factors such as government policies. Our results show that user authority plays a crucial role in shaping medical information sharing and that it has a different effect on different types of information, and that it varies across communities and time. Furthermore, our research finds that stricter government controls on information sharing lead to increased user authority and thus greater spread of information, although this may come at the cost of increased misinformation. Overall, our findings have important implications for how medical information is managed and regulated in China, and our research provides a framework for studying online information sharing that can be applied to other domains. A systematic search for planetary nebulae was conducted using data from the VLT/MUSE spectrograph as part of the Fornax3D survey.  The observations, spanning 0.5 arcmin^2 around the center of early-type galaxies in the Fornax cluster, yielded 845 detected planetary nebulae with a median excitation line flux of 10^-17 erg s^-1 cm^-2. The nebulae's physical distances from their host galaxies' centers could be estimated statistically, with the average distance ranging from 20 to 60 kpc. The observed planetary nebulae populations correlate with the brightness and distribution of the underlying light within the galaxies. The nebulae's detection frequency also decreases with increasing stellar mass. The main challenge in identifying the planetary nebulae was minimizing false positives, primarily caused by the presence of [O III] emission from stellar nuclei. The false positive rate was minimized by implementing a set of criteria based on the nebulae's morphology, spectral slope, and line strength ratio. The resulting catalog includes the coordinates, line fluxes, line strengths, nebulae's excitation state, physical distance from the galaxy's center, and likelihood of each object being a genuine planetary nebula. The most reliable 60% of the detections are considered high-confidence planetary nebulae, with the remaining 40% classified as probable nebulae. The accuracy of the distance measurements was validated by comparing the nebulae associated with the galaxy NGC 1316 to those found in the literature, with the results showing the method's effectiveness. To address this gap, we present LifeStream, a WF-SPPE designed to efficiently process periodic flows with unlimited duration.
LifeStream achieves high efficiency by utilizing a hybrid approach that combines iterative computations and continuous aggregation, allowing for significant reductions in memory usage, processing time, and window sizes.

Continuous-phase modulation (CPM) has gained popularity due to its resistance to frequency-selective fading and coherent detection's reduced requirements. A key advantage of CPM is its ability to withstand carrier phase ambiguity. However, its limited differential delay makes it prone to timing synchronization problems in certain applications. To address this issue, this paper focuses on expanding the differential delay of CPM by designing a new metric that can tolerate longer carrier phase ambiguities. This new criterion takes into account both the intrinsic differential delay and the minimum distance between CPM symbols. By controlling this new metric, we can effectively manage the differential delay and increase it without sacrificing the minimum distance between symbols. In a Rayleigh fading channel with carrier phase ambiguity, this results in almost error-free detection performance for CPM signals with an extended differential delay. This extension is particularly notable for CPM signals with orthogonal differentials, where CPM signals with C^2 = 2^m - 1 (rather than 2^m) can be reliably detected. This improvement is demonstrated in an experiment using BPSK, QPSK, and 8PSK CPM signals in a mobile fading channel. This extra differential delay allows for increased delay times, allowing for the detection of signals with longer dwell times in applications like molecular communication systems. This additional delay also allows for the use of more complex signals, like 8PSK CPM, in environments with shorter dwell times. This research shows that designing CPM signals with larger differential delays results in reliable detection in applications with carrier phase ambiguity, providing a practical guideline for future CPM signal design. This atlas covers a wide range of common sense reasoning expressed as "if-then" statements, encompassing various situations, emotions, and relationships involved in social interactions. By analyzing 200,000 text samples from the Commonsense Knowledge Question Answering Dataset, ATOMIC extracts 150,000 relevant statements. Our findings highlight the complexity of this knowledge base, revealing that the majority of statements are condition-independent, often reflecting general principles such as fairness and accuracy, while approximately 20% contain biased conditions that can influence conclusions, potentially leading to biased outcomes. By offering pre-trained models to perform if-then reasoning on this massive scale, ATOMIC facilitates in-depth analysis of these statements and the atlas itself, providing valuable insights into the nature of machine common knowledge. Our work paves the way for developing more sophisticated evaluation methods and a deeper understanding of the limitations and potential biases in large language models. By sharing our findings and the ATOMIC atlas with the community, we aim to accelerate progress in areas like natural language inference and machine common knowledge. Our code and database are available at https://atomi.github.io/.

When conditioned on a specific task, it results in target-oriented multi-modal training. Experimental evaluations have shown that the proposed bidirectional focus method leads to significant improvements in speech recognition performance, and when conditioned on a speaker, it achieves a relative error rate reduction of 6.4\% in the WER, and when conditioned on a specific task, it achieves a relative error rate reduction of 8.5\% in the WER. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of a specific parameter, denoted as $N_k$, which represents the number of leading digits of a certain class of integer vectors in base $b$. These integer vectors are derived from uniform parking functions in a process that involves a transformation defined by a specific polynomial, and their leading digits are determined after a process of modulo $b-1$ reduction. We establish that for a specific range of base values, $b_k$ is consistently $k+1$, and through the use of a more general model, we show that the sequence $N_k$ converges to $(b-1)\cdot \lambda^{\lambda-1}/\Gamma(\lambda)$ for a given $\lambda$, which is approximately $e$ when considering the context of base $b$. This allows us to determine the asymptotic distribution of $N_k$ as an extension of the normal distribution. Additionally, we discuss an alternative approach using the branching process, its underlying tree structure, and the concept of a zone of depth $\lambda$ to provide further insights into the behavior of $N_k$. This approach enables us to interpret the value of $\lambda$ as an indicator of the level of branching in the tree and thus the level of asymptotic distribution for the sequence $N_k$. Researchers investigated the conductivity of superconducting nanowires made of niobium nitride under external gate voltage control. They employed an experimental setup that allowed for real-time measurement of conductivity and voltage across the nanowire. Interesting phenomena observed include persistent conductance states, fluctuations in conductance, and rare occurrences of complete blockage of conductance. The study focuses on a specific phase conductance was confined to extremely low values and could only be restored by applying a large voltage. There are two possible explanations for this behavior: the occurrence of coherent quantum phase slips or a phenomenon known as Coulomb obstruction. To better understand the findings, researchers analyzed the behavior of single vortices within the nanowire by creating a situation where only one vortex existed. This was achieved by heating the nanowire above its superconducting temperature, allowing the vortex to form spontaneously, and then cooling it below its superconducting temperature. The resulting data showed that at low temperatures, the energy required to create a vortex was equivalent to the energy of two electrons. This value is known to be precise for a specific type of vortex known as a "core vortex". However, there are other types of vortices that could have different energies. The occurrence of conductance states at specific gate voltages could be linked to the formation of these other types of vortices. The data also revealed that the energy required to move the vortex to a different position within the nanowire was equivalent to the energy of four electrons. This is equivalent to the energy of two vortices, thereby confirming that the behavior observed was indeed the result of a single moving vortex. The data further indicates that the conductance states and blockages observed were directly linked to the formation of this single moving vortex. In applications such as video surveillance, view changes can result in the inconvenience of switching between multiple cameras to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the evolving situation. Recent research introduced the novel problem of innovative view video forecasting, which predicts the existence and content of unobserved cameras. Current methods primarily focus on related view video prediction, ignoring the possibility of novel views. Our work addresses this challenge by developing an end-to-end framework that can distinguish between novel and existing views, along with predicting their contents. The proposed model consists of a dual representation, incorporating both spatial and temporal features that enables the network to generate both related and novel views. Experimental evaluation in a simulated environment demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach. Moreover, our model is applied to real-world data and yields promising results in both novel and related view prediction. The code is available online at https://github.com/ghrashid95/Dual-View-Video-Forecasting.

To facilitate comparison, our results are also compared with analogous solutions derived using the Caputo fractional derivative. To address the mystery surrounding the third generation's overproduction, a vector leptoquark is proposed as an explanation. To accommodate the "missing third generation" phenomenon, this leptoquark must couple primarily to first- or second-generation particles. However, if it's assumed that a specific type of vector leptoquark with charge $5/3$ predominately produces top-quark pairs or same-flavor dileptons with nucleons, it would actually overproduces the third generation. On the other hand, it's predicted that such a leptoquark would likely produce same-sign dilepton pairs with significant transverse momentum, particularly in proton-proton collisions at higher energies, such as those used in LHC Run 2 or future experiments. By utilizing the method of integration by parts, the development of a general expression for the production of same-sign dilepton pairs in this vector leptoquark framework is facilitated, with the calculation of the hard cross-section completed to the level of its coefficients. As a result, with the inclusion of radiative corrections and the simulation of hadronization and decay, a comprehensive event generator becomes available for the production of same-sign dilepton pairs in this vector leptoquark framework. Based on an estimation of hadronization and decay effects, it's estimated that the hard cross-section for the production of same-sign muon pairs in this vector leptoquark framework is approximately $0.59 \pm 0.05$ nb in proton-proton collisions at an energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13.6$ TeV. With the inclusion of radiative corrections, this amount is found to be $0.64^{+0.09}_{-0.07} \pm 0.05$ nb in proton-proton collisions at an energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13.6$ TeV. Similarly, the hard cross-section for the production of same-sign electron pairs in this vector leptoquark framework is found to be $4.9^{+0.7}_{-0.6} \pm 0.4$ nb in proton-proton collisions at an energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13.6$ TeV. With the inclusion of radiative corrections, this amount is found to be $5.4^{+0.8}_{-0.7} \pm 0.4$ nb in proton-proton collisions at an energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13.6$ TeV.

When combined with the neural network, a physics-based optimization algorithm reduced noise in low-dose PET scans while achieving performance comparable to current state-of-the-art optimization techniques. When using standard-dose MRI scans, the algorithm successfully reconstructed high-quality PET images from heavily compressed data sets, as well as image sets modified by common artifacts. When trained to distinguish between healthy tissue and tumors with low-dose PET images and MRI scans, the network accurately identified cancerous tissues with low error rates, even when trained with data sets different from the original training set. When combined with the neural network, the algorithm successfully reconstructed high-quality PET images from highly compressed data sets, as well as image sets modified by common artifacts. The developed framework has the potential to reduce the costs and risks associated with whole-body PET scans. The beam disruption effect causes electrical fluctuations in a particle accelerator's equipment when it encounters unwanted beam particles. In Energy Recovery Linacs, where one beam particle carries energy in one direction while another particle carries it in the opposite direction, this issue is particularly pronounced and affects the stability of future machines. The beam disruption effect has distinct consequences on the electrical system, influencing the stability boundary and, as a result, affect the initial conditions that determine when instability occurs. Until now, research has focused on a specific situation where the beam particles' energy characteristics are identical and the filling configuration of beam particles was ignored. This study investigates the impact of different beam particle energy characteristics and filling configurations on the stability limit, revealing the significant influence they have, and demonstrating that the instability's threshold can vary significantly, ultimately affecting the initial conditions that lead to instability. As a result, addressing this issue will require careful planning and control of the beam particles' energy characteristics and filling configurations, among other factors. This research was conducted to examine a specific machine, but its findings are likely to be applicable to other Energy Recovery Linacs facing a similar beam disruption instability problem.
